docs.title: Elenchus (ἔλεγχος)
docs.text:
Real-time Socratic debate analysis and fallacy detection engine for live conversations and recorded speech.

Elenchus runs on your local machine. It listens to desktop audio or microphone input, transcribes spoken statements with faster-whisper, spots logical fallacies with a local LLM through Ollama, and displays short refutations in a translucent desktop HUD.

← Return to Main Website & Live Simulator

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Offline and private: Audio transcription and reasoning run locally in volatile memory with zero external network requests.
  • Low latency: Local CPU speech recognition paired with quantized language models for real-time turnarounds during live speech.
  • Desktop HUD: Frameless, translucent desktop overlay that stays visible above active windows without stealing input focus.
  • Rhetorical pre-filtering: Discards conversational filler, background noise, and incomplete utterances before fallacy evaluation.
  • Cross-platform: Prebuilt standalone packages and quick-start scripts across Windows, macOS, and Linux.

docs.title: System architecture
docs.text: This document outlines the internal pipeline, data flow, threading structure, and error handling for Elenchus.

docs.title: Pipeline overview
docs.text:
Elenchus breaks speech analysis into four decoupled stages running entirely on local CPU and GPU cores without network calls:

flowchart TD
    A["Audio Input<br/><small>Mic or WASAPI Loopback</small>"] -->|"Raw float32 audio"| B["Stage 1: Ingestion & VAD<br/><small>Voice Activity Detection</small>"]
    B -->|"Discrete speech slice"| C["Stage 2: Speech-to-Text<br/><small>faster-whisper INT8</small>"]
    C -->|"Transcript string"| D["Proposition Pre-Filter<br/><small>Heuristic Filter</small>"]
    D -->|"Validated argument claim"| E["Stage 3: Fallacy Engine<br/><small>Ollama Local Model</small>"]
    E -->|"Classification & counter"| F["Stage 4: Desktop Overlay<br/><small>PyQt6 HUD Window</small>"]

docs.title: Data flow and stage handoffs
docs.text:
Here is how audio and text move through volatile memory:

  • Input to Stage 1: Incoming audio arrives in 16 kHz mono chunks from PortAudio or WASAPI loopback. The VAD calculates root-mean-square (RMS) energy to separate deliberate speech from background room noise.
  • Stage 1 to Stage 2: When silence is detected (or push-to-talk is released), the accumulated speech slice in RAM is dispatched directly to the faster-whisper worker thread.
  • Stage 2 to Stage 3 (The Proposition Pre-Filter): Transcribing speech is not enough. People pause, cough, repeat words, and make conversational interjections. The heuristic filter evaluates whether the transcript forms a complete claim before sending it to the LLM. If the text is conversational noise, it gets discarded. This prevents the model from hallucinating fallacies on throat-clearing.
  • Stage 3 to Stage 4: When a complete claim exists, the local model checks for formal and informal fallacies. It returns an explanation and a counter-argument under 30 words.
  • At Stage 4: The PyQt6 HUD receives a thread-safe Qt signal with the verdict, the counter-argument, and the latency telemetry, displaying it in your peripheral field of view.

docs.title: Stage 1: Audio ingestion and voice activity detection
docs.text:
Implemented in core.audio_capture and core.vad.

The recorder captures raw float32 audio at 16 kHz mono from default microphones or loopback streams (WASAPI on Windows, PulseAudio or PipeWire monitor on Linux). Voice activity detection supports two styles: manual push-to-talk and continuous RMS energy tracking with a rolling noise floor.

Audio arrays remain strictly in volatile RAM. Nothing is ever written to disk.

docs.title: Stage 2: Quantized speech recognition
docs.text:
Implemented in core.transcriber.

Speech recognition runs on faster-whisper using the base.en model quantized to INT8. It runs across 4 CPU threads with a beam size of 1 to keep latency minimal. The transcriber cleans up repeated words, silence padding, and coughing in quick bursts under 500 ms.

docs.title: Stage 3: Fallacy classification
docs.text:
Implemented in core.llm_client.

Classification relies on a local Ollama daemon running lightweight quantized reasoning models, defaulting to qwen2.5-coder:3b.

Before sending text to the model, an argument proposition filter evaluates whether the transcript forms a complete claim. If the speaker paused mid-sentence, cleared their throat, or uttered filler words, the pipeline discards the text. When a genuine claim arrives, the model identifies any formal or informal fallacy and returns a counter-argument under 30 words.

docs.title: Stage 4: Desktop HUD overlay
docs.text:
Implemented in ui.overlay and ui.waveform.

The interface is a hardware-accelerated PyQt6 window marked with Qt.WindowStaysOnTopHint. The window hovers over full-screen apps without stealing keyboard focus. It shows live Monochart audio meters, status LEDs, and latency timestamps.

For operating instructions, status indicators, and hotkey controls, see the User guide. For memory allocation budgets and latency telemetry, see the Runtime specifications.

docs.title: Concurrency and thread isolation
docs.text:
To keep the interface responsive at 60 FPS while models are running, Elenchus splits work into three execution contexts:

Thread Context Responsibilities Thread 0 (UI Thread) PyQt6 Event Loop Handles paint events, window dragging, key inputs, and widget re-renders. Never blocks on I/O. Audio Recorder Thread PortAudio / sounddevice High-priority ring-buffer callback continuously reading incoming hardware chunks into an internal queue. Pipeline Coordinator Dedicated QThread Reads audio chunks, computes RMS energy, runs faster-whisper, queries Ollama via local HTTP, and emits thread-safe Qt signals (result_ready, audio_level).

docs.title: Sample rate negotiation
docs.text: Most consumer microphones and virtual audio outputs run at 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz. Elenchus queries the native endpoint and resamples the stream to 16 kHz in memory using linear interpolation, avoiding pitch warping.

docs.title: Ollama service handling
docs.text: If the Ollama daemon crashes or stops mid-session, network exceptions are caught immediately. The HUD switches to a red warning LED rather than freezing the Qt event loop.

docs.title: Shutdown and cleanup
docs.text: When closing the application, closeEvent joins background worker threads, closes active stream descriptors, and releases PortAudio handles so no orphaned processes linger.

docs.title: Version scopes and roadmap
docs.text:
This document defines scope boundaries and milestone deliverables for each version of Elenchus under Semantic Versioning.

Historical release notes, commit logs, and downloadable assets are published on GitHub Releases.

docs.title: Version index
docs.text: Version Milestone Status Scope summary v1.0.0 Core engine and desktop HUD Stable Offline speech recognition, Ollama fallacy reasoning, and floating PyQt6 HUD overlay. v1.1.0 Standalone binary distribution In progress Zero-dependency standalone executables for Windows, macOS, and Linux with automated release packaging. v1.2.0 Extended debate analytics Planned Multi-speaker recording sessions up to 30 minutes, full transcript analysis, and personal fallacy trends.

docs.title: v1.0.0: Core engine and desktop HUD (stable)
docs.text: The initial release establishes the local sparring loop. You speak (or route incoming call audio), the engine transcribes the claim on CPU, checks for logical fallacies locally, and displays a concise counter-argument in the overlay.

docs.title: Scope boundaries
docs.text:
• Audio input records 16 kHz mono streams from default microphones or system loopback (WASAPI on Windows, PulseAudio or PipeWire on Linux).
  • Voice detection supports manual push-to-talk toggling and automated RMS energy detection with silence timeouts.
  • Speech transcription runs on CPU via faster-whisper using INT8 quantization, using zero GPU memory.
  • A heuristic pre-filter drops conversational filler, mid-sentence pauses, and coughs before calling the model.
  • Fallacy reasoning runs locally through Ollama using qwen2.5-coder:3b, returning classifications and refutations under 30 words.
  • The interface is a frameless, translucent PyQt6 desktop overlay with real-time audio meters and status lights.
  • Developers can clone and run the project directly using Astral uv (uv run elenchus).

docs.title: Excluded from v1.0.0
docs.text:
This milestone does not include standalone compiled installers without Python, continuous multi-speaker transcripts across long sessions, or remote cloud model synchronization.

Full patch notes and release artifacts are documented on GitHub Release v1.0.0.

docs.title: v1.1.0: Standalone binary distribution (in progress)
docs.text: The second milestone eliminates developer tool dependencies so anyone can install and run Elenchus with a single double-click or terminal command.

docs.title: Scope boundaries
docs.text:
• Standalone executables for Windows (x86_64), macOS (arm64 and x86_64), and Linux (x86_64) that run without Python preinstalled.
  • Automated GitHub Actions workflows that compile release binaries, compute SHA-256 digests, and attach assets to tagged release drafts.
  • Single-command web installers for PowerShell and Bash that verify hashes and place the binary on the user path.
  • Initial groundwork for native distribution channels (winget, Scoop, Homebrew, and Flatpak).

docs.title: Excluded from v1.1.0
docs.text: Long debate recording sessions remain scheduled for v1.2.0. This release avoids UI overhauls to focus entirely on distribution and packaging reliability.

docs.title: v1.2.0: Extended debate analytics (planned)
docs.text: The third milestone expands Elenchus from real-time single-claim sparring into comprehensive debate session analysis.

docs.title: Scope boundaries
docs.text:
• Long-format audio ingestion accepting up to 30 minutes of recorded debate audio, generating per-statement fallacy breakdowns.
  • Opponent audio isolation to analyze both speakers separately during Discord or browser conference calls.
  • Optional integration with macOS's built-in speech engine for lower memory usage on Apple Silicon.
  • A local fallacy history tracker that identifies recurring cognitive patterns across multiple sessions.

docs.title: Installation and distribution
docs.text: Elenchus provides prebuilt standalone binaries with SHA-256 integrity verification, along with an Astral uv setup for running directly from source.

docs.title: Single-command installers
docs.text:
Windows (PowerShell)macOS (Apple Silicon)macOS (Intel)Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Arch)

Open PowerShell and run:

irm https://github.com/Asifdotexe/elenchus/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex
  • Saves elenchus-windows-x86_64.exe into $env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\Elenchus\
  • Verifies the SHA-256 checksum against the release digest
  • Adds the binary to your user PATH

Open Terminal and run:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/Asifdotexe/elenchus/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
  • Downloads elenchus-darwin-arm64 (native M1 to M4) into ~/.local/bin/elenchus
  • Checks the SHA-256 checksum against the release digest
  • Marks the file executable (chmod +x)

Open Terminal and run:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/Asifdotexe/elenchus/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
  • Detects x86_64 architecture and downloads elenchus-darwin-x86_64
  • Verifies the SHA-256 checksum and installs to ~/.local/bin/elenchus

Open Terminal and run:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/Asifdotexe/elenchus/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
  • Downloads elenchus-linux-x86_64 to ~/.local/bin/elenchus
  • Checks the release checksum and sets executable permissions

docs.title: Standalone binary packages
docs.text:
If you work in airgapped environments or prefer manual installs, download the binaries directly from GitHub Releases.

Platform Architecture Release file Integrity check Default path Windows (64-bit) x86_64 elenchus-windows-x86_64.exe SHA-256 verified %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Elenchus\ macOS (Apple Silicon) arm64 (M1 to M4) elenchus-darwin-arm64 SHA-256 verified ~/.local/bin/elenchus macOS (Intel) x86_64 elenchus-darwin-x86_64 SHA-256 verified ~/.local/bin/elenchus Linux (glibc 2.31+) x86_64 elenchus-linux-x86_64 SHA-256 verified ~/.local/bin/elenchus

docs.title: Manual verification
docs.text:
To check the hash of a downloaded binary yourself:

Windows (PowerShell): 

Get-FileHash .\elenchus-windows-x86_64.exe -Algorithm SHA256

macOS: 

shasum -a 256 elenchus-darwin-arm64

Linux: 

sha256sum elenchus-linux-x86_64

Compare the output hash with the values listed in checksums.txt on the release page.

docs.title: Running from source
docs.text: If you want to modify Elenchus or inspect the code, run it through Astral uv:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or newer
  • Astral uv (curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh or irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex)
  • Ollama installed and running locally

docs.title: Clone and run
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Asifdotexe/elenchus.git
cd elenchus

# uv sets up the virtual environment and starts the app
uv run elenchus

docs.title: Pull an Ollama model
docs.text:
Elenchus defaults to fast, lightweight models to keep latency low:

ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:3b
# Alternatively:
ollama pull qwen2.5:3b

To configure alternative models or adjust endpoints, see Ollama configuration. For model latency impacts, see Latency budget breakdown.

docs.title: Design philosophy and origins
docs.text: "For the love of the game. I honestly enjoy debates, but there is a huge difference between a heated argument and a well-structured discussion, and it comes down to how someone puts out their statement." Asif Sayyed, project creator in his journal

docs.title: What is Elenchus?
docs.text:
Elenchus takes its name from the ancient Greek term ἔλεγχος (élenkhos), the Socratic method of argumentative dialogue. In Socratic dialogue, the point is never to shout louder or win through theatrical rhetoric. The point is to test claims, pull apart premises, and see whether a conclusion actually holds up.

Elenchus is a small HUD tool that floats on your desktop. It listens to spoken statements from your microphone or audio loopback, breaks each sentence down into premises and conclusions, and checks whether a fallacy was committed, providing a quick explanation of why.

An additional nicety: it requires no token costs and runs completely offline in a lightweight manner.

docs.title: For the love of the game
docs.text:
Good debates are rare. Most disagreements turn into shouting matches where both sides talk past each other, move goalposts, and attack character instead of evidence.

In debates, people can be disingenuous. Sometimes they do it on purpose to win an exchange, but just as often it happens by accident because human thinking naturally takes shortcuts. Having a clear, real-time read on whether a statement is structurally valid helps weed out poor arguments and debates with no end.

When you can see the logical structure underneath the emotion of an argument, two things happen:

  1. You make sounder, more robust arguments: You catch your own unsupported leaps and shaky premises before you say them out loud.
  2. You smell unsound or half-baked arguments immediately: You notice when an opponent swaps definitions, sets up a straw man, or forces a false dilemma, and you know exactly where their reasoning failed.

docs.title: A sparring partner, not a replacement brain
docs.text:
A central question that came up during early development was:

"The aim of the tool is to learn. Having an assist of this sort shouldn't lead to people offloading their cognitive ability."

That distinction matters. If software generates your debate responses for you, your own rhetorical skills get worse. You become passive and dependent on an automated crutch.

Elenchus is built as an intellectual sparring partner, not an autonomous brain:

Cognitive offloading (unhelpful) Cognitive elevation (our approach) AI generates entire speeches You form your own argument You become a passive reader The HUD highlights logical fallacies Rhetorical instincts atrophy over time You read the rationale and understand the flaw Creates reliance on external models Your brain learns the pattern and reacts faster

When boxers train on a heavy bag or work with a sparring partner, the partner does not step into the ring on fight night. The partner helps build reflexes so that during the real fight, muscle memory takes over. Elenchus works the same way for your thinking.

docs.title: What is under the HUD (pun intended)
1. Zero token cost, zero clouds
docs.text:
Debate practice should not carry an API bill, and private conversations should never leave your machine.

Every audio buffer stays strictly in volatile memory, speech transcription runs on CPU without using VRAM, and model inference executes entirely on your local GPU. For detailed memory allocations and latency telemetry, see the canonical Hardware allocation budget and Latency budget breakdown.

docs.title: 2. Why a coder model? Brevity
docs.text:
General chat models tend to produce three-paragraph essays. While listening to someone in a live conversation, you do not have time to read an essay.

I chose qwen2.5-coder:3b specifically because coder models give concise, structured responses. The task of classifying a premise is simple enough for a coder model, and its rationale has brevity. Rebuttals stay under 30 words, formatted so you can glance at them in a fraction of a second without losing eye contact or your train of thought. For technical implementation details, see Stage 3: Fallacy classification.

docs.title: 3. A floating desktop HUD
docs.text:
Rather than burying the tool in a browser tab or terminal window, Elenchus uses a translucent PyQt6 overlay pinned over your active desktop apps (Zoom, Discord, browser, or terminal). It stays visible in your peripheral field of view when you need it and fades into the background when you do not.

For window controls, status LEDs, and shortcuts, see the User guide.

docs.title: How do I distribute? Simplicity and ease of use
docs.text:
Software should be as straightforward to install as it is to run. Rather than requiring everyone to configure Python environments or shell scripts, distribution is tiered across standalone binaries, quick-start commands, and editable source builds.

For command-line installers, manual verification hashes, and source setup, see Installation and distribution.

docs.title: Future evolution
docs.text:
The core release provides a baseline sparring loop for single statements. Exploratory capabilities from the development journal (such as extended session recordings, opponent audio isolation, and personal argument metrics) are planned as version milestones.

For scope boundaries and planned version targets, see Version scopes and roadmap.

docs.title: Runtime specifications and benchmarks
docs.text: This page is the canonical reference for performance metrics, latency budgets, hardware memory footprints, and baseline requirements for Elenchus.

docs.title: Core manifesto
docs.text:
Conversations move faster than memory.

When an opponent in a live debate shifts premises, forces a false dilemma, or attacks character instead of evidence, you often catch the flaw seconds after your turn to respond has passed.

Elenchus runs quietly in the background. It listens to incoming speech, evaluates logical claims, and shows short Socratic counter-arguments directly in your peripheral vision before you take your turn to speak.

docs.title: Verified benchmarks
docs.text:
These numbers reflect verified runs on mid-tier consumer hardware (Intel Core i5-11400 or AMD Ryzen 5 5600X, 16 GB RAM, RTX 3060):

Metric Target Measurement method Peak resident memory (RAM) < 380 MB RSS Task Manager / /proc/[pid]/status during INT8 CPU transcription Speech chunk STT latency ~ 550 ms Timestamp delta between audio chunk completion and text emission LLM classification latency 650 ms to 950 ms Ollama response latency using qwen2.5-coder:3b (Q4_K_M) End-to-end latency < 2.5 seconds Time from end of speech slice to counter-argument rendered in HUD External network transmission 0 bytes Verified with Wireshark and Process Hacker (fully offline) Binary digest integrity SHA-256 Automated digest check against release checksums.txt

docs.title: Hardware allocation budget
docs.text:
Elenchus is budgeted to run on machines with modest headroom without starving active video calls, browsers, or streaming software:

pie title Hardware memory footprint by component (~3.0 GB total)
    "Ollama LLM (2200 MB VRAM)" : 2200
    "faster-whisper STT (650 MB RAM)" : 650
    "PyQt6 HUD overlay (80 MB RAM)" : 80
    "Audio capture & VAD (50 MB RAM)" : 50
Subsystem Component Hardware target Memory budget Share Purpose Audio capture & VAD sounddevice + numpy Host CPU < 50 MB RAM 1.7% 16 kHz audio buffer and energy thresholding Speech-to-text faster-whisper (base.en) CPU (INT8, 4 threads) ~ 650 MB RAM 21.8% Quantized INT8 weights in system RAM (0 MB VRAM) Desktop HUD overlay PyQt6 composited window CPU / Compositor < 80 MB RAM 2.7% Transparent obsidian HUD elements Debate reasoning qwen2.5-coder:3b Dedicated GPU ~ 2,200 MB VRAM 73.8% 4-bit quantized model resident in VRAM Total memory footprint All subsystems Hybrid RAM + VRAM ~ 2,980 MB 100% Leaves ample headroom for Discord, OBS, or Zoom

System RAM stays under 800 MB RSS during continuous speech recognition. The LLM reasoning model runs isolated in ~2.2 GB of GPU VRAM, keeping desktop multitasking fluid.

docs.title: Latency budget breakdown
docs.text:
Elenchus targets an end-to-end response time under 2.5 seconds, with a typical turnaround of ~1.55 seconds (1,550 ms) on recommended hardware:

pie title Latency share by pipeline stage (1.55s total)
    "Ollama local inference (0.80s)" : 800
    "faster-whisper STT (0.55s)" : 550
    "Audio buffer & VAD cutoff (0.10s)" : 100
    "Argument pre-filter (0.05s)" : 50
    "PyQt6 HUD repaint (0.05s)" : 50
Pipeline stage Duration Latency Budget share Purpose Stage 1: Buffer flush & VAD cutoff 0.10s 100 ms 6.5% Audio ring buffer capture and energy thresholding Stage 2: Speech-to-text 0.55s 550 ms 35.5% faster-whisper INT8 CPU transcription Proposition pre-filter 0.05s 50 ms 3.2% Rejects incomplete utterances, stutters, and room noise Stage 3: Fallacy & refutation engine 0.80s 800 ms 51.6% Ollama local model inference (qwen2.5-coder:3b) Stage 4: Desktop HUD repaint 0.05s 50 ms 3.2% PyQt6 thread-safe signal dispatch and widget repaint Total end-to-end turnaround ~1.55s 1,550 ms 100% Refutation displayed before your speaking turn

Over 87 percent of total processing time is dedicated to local AI execution (0.80 seconds for Ollama refutation generation and 0.55 seconds for faster-whisper speech transcription). Audio ingestion, heuristics, and UI compositing take less than 0.20 seconds combined (under 13 percent), ensuring zero sluggishness on the desktop.

docs.title: User guide and HUD controls
docs.text: This guide covers how to position the desktop overlay, select audio devices, choose voice detection modes, and configure local Ollama models.

docs.title: Operating the desktop HUD
docs.text: The Elenchus overlay is a minimal, translucent window designed to stay in your peripheral vision during live calls without blocking other windows.

docs.title: Moving and positioning
docs.text:
• Click and drag anywhere on the HUD header or background to move it across monitors.
  • The window sets Qt.WindowStaysOnTopHint, keeping it visible when other apps (Discord, Zoom, Google Meet) have focus.

docs.title: Status indicators
docs.text:
• Green LED (#98ff38): Ready and listening for spoken statements.
  • Amber LED (#d97706): Transcribing audio or running fallacy inference.
  • Red LED (#ef4444): Warning state (such as an unreachable Ollama instance).

docs.title: Audio waveform meter
docs.text: The Monochart energy meter shows incoming audio amplitude in real time. Bars illuminate green once voice energy rises above the baseline noise floor.

docs.title: Voice activity detection modes
docs.text: Elenchus supports two listening modes depending on your setting:

docs.title: Manual push-to-talk (recommended for debates)
docs.text:
• Click the HUD action bar or press Space to start recording when your opponent speaks. Click again when they finish.
  • This avoids background noise, interruptions, or coughing from triggering unneeded model runs.

docs.title: Continuous automatic VAD
docs.text:
• The engine calculates real-time RMS energy automatically.
  • When speech remains above the noise threshold for 300 ms, recording starts. When silence persists for 700 ms, the audio slice sends to the transcriber.
  • Useful for hands-free listening.

docs.title: Capturing opponent audio with loopback
docs.text:
To analyze an opponent over Discord or a web browser on Windows:

  1. Set your system output to your normal headphones or speakers.
  2. In config.py (or through --device in the CLI), pick the loopback endpoint matching your output device.
  3. Elenchus captures the WASAPI loopback stream directly without needing virtual audio cable drivers.

docs.title: Capturing microphone audio
docs.text: To practice statements yourself or analyze an in-person room debate, select your physical USB microphone or headset input in config.py.

docs.title: Ollama configuration
docs.text: Elenchus communicates with your local Ollama daemon at http://localhost:11434.

docs.title: Switching models
docs.text:
Specify your preferred model in config.py:

# Default model for concise fallacy detection
OLLAMA_MODEL = "qwen2.5-coder:3b"

Tested options:

  • qwen2.5-coder:3b (default): Fast inference and reliable on informal fallacy detection with concise phrasing.
  • qwen2.5:3b: Good general reasoning alternative.
  • llama3.2:3b: Lightweight alternative with low memory usage.
  • mistral:7b: Provides longer, more nuanced refutations at higher VRAM usage.

For benchmark comparisons and latency breakdown, see Runtime specifications. For the design rationale behind selecting coder models, see Why a coder model? Brevity.

docs.title: Starting Ollama
docs.text:
Make sure Ollama is running before starting Elenchus: 

ollama list
If it is not running, start it in a separate terminal: 
ollama serve
